subtype: Approach: testing repeatedly and logging failures [Action]
passage: I'm Lalit. Hrithik and I ran our robot fifty times on the mock track and wrote every failure in a log: run number, what went wrong, our guess at why. Twenty-two of the fifty were the same thing, the left wheel wobbling loose. Eleven were sensor glare from the window. The rest looked random, and nobody wanted to chase the random ones. So we tightened the wheel, checked every screw before each run, and taped a card over the sensor as a shade. Then we ran fifty more. Forty-one finished. Looking back, the log changed how I felt about failing: from it keeps going wrong to here is the list, and we can fix number one first.

qa.q: How many of the fifty runs failed because of the loose left wheel?
qa.a: Twenty-two of the fifty were the wobbling left wheel.

qa.q: How did the log change what Lalit felt about the failures?
qa.a: Lalit went from feeling stuck to feeling hopeful, since a written list made the problems fixable one at a time.

qa.q: What else could the team try?
qa.a: They could test at different times of day or in another room to check the glare problem, and keep logging the results.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see the log?
qa.a: Hrithik may feel relieved to have evidence instead of arguments, since Hrithik helped run the tests and record them.

grounding: Students run the robot fifty times on a mock track, log each failure and cause, and fix the most frequent problem first, such as a loose wheel or sensor glare.

passage:
Robotics coach's notes, week 6.
Suraj and Reena set up the mock track in the corridor after school and ran the robot fifty times. Reena kept the log in a ruled notebook: run number, where it failed, what they thought caused it. By run twenty Suraj wanted to stop and "just fix everything," but Reena kept going. When they totalled it, 19 of the 50 runs had failed. Eleven failures were at the curve under the corridor window, where sunlight hit the track and the sensor lost the line. Five were a wheel slipping; three were a low battery. They taped a small cardboard hood over the sensor first, since that was the biggest problem. The next twenty runs had two failures.
What I did next: I moved the mock track to a spot that gets strong afternoon sun on purpose, so they can test the fix in the worst light.

qa.q: How many of the fifty runs failed?
How was Suraj feeling around run twenty?
qa.a: Suraj felt impatient and wanted to stop and just fix everything, while Reena kept going.

qa.q: What should they fix after the sensor hood, and why?
qa.a: The slipping wheel, since it caused the next most failures; then another round of runs will show what remains.

qa.q: How might Reena see the log after they totalled it?
qa.a: Reena likely feels vindicated, since the notebook showed the sunny curve caused most failures and gave them a clear first fix.

grounding: Shows students running a robot fifty times on a mock track, logging each failure and cause, and fixing the most frequent problem, sensor glare, first.

passage:
Saturday
Fifty runs today on the practice mat in Joseph's garage. My arm aches from resetting the robot. Joseph thought it was pointless ("it works, Urmi, we've seen it work"), but I made him call out each failure while I wrote it down.
Tally by 6 pm:
left wheel wobbling off: 9
missed the black line at the sharp turn: 4
stopped for no reason: 2
Fifteen fails out of fifty. And more than half of them are the same silly wheel! I would never have guessed. I thought the turn was our big problem.
Joseph tightened the grub screw and added a drop of glue. We ran ten more before his mum called us for dinner: zero wheel falls. 😊
Tomorrow: the sharp turn.
Urmila

qa.q: How many times did the left wheel wobble off?
qa.a: The left wheel wobbled off 9 times.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel on seeing the tally?
qa.a: Urmila was surprised and a bit exasperated that the same wheel caused more than half the fails, not the turn.

qa.q: What would you tackle next, and why?
qa.a: The sharp turn, since it now causes the most fails; running and logging another set will show whether both fixes hold.

qa.q: How might Joseph see the fifty runs now?
qa.a: Joseph thought testing was pointless, but zero wheel falls after his fix likely show him why the log mattered.

grounding: Illustrates students running fifty test runs, logging each failure and cause, and fixing the most frequent one, a loose wheel, first.
